title: Learn from Your Decisions
hook: Teresa's winning stock pick is the most dangerous item on the investment club table.
counterintuition: A good result can feel like proof even though it may only be luck in a convincing costume. Learn from the process before you update the rule.
tryThisNow: Pick one recent outcome and split the page into process, result, and noise. Write one rule you would keep, change, or ignore.
keyTakeaway: Learning from decisions means separating process quality from outcome noise before turning experience into a new rule.

breakdown.fastRead:
The receipt paper curls beside Teresa's coffee cup as the investment club cheers the stock that doubled. Everyone wants to repeat the rule: buy when the founder gives a confident interview. Teresa stops them. The pick made money, but the purchase notes show no margin, no comparison, and no check on the balance sheet.

A lucky win can become an expensive teacher.

Teresa writes three headings: process, result, noise. The result was good. The process was weak. The lesson is not to trust confident founders. The lesson is to avoid confusing a profitable accident with a rule worth repeating.
breakdown.deepRead:
At 7:30 Monday, Rosa opens the surgery scheduling audit and sees one ugly number: three delayed cases last Friday. The easy lesson is that the new schedule failed. Then she reads the notes. One surgeon had an emergency add-on, one patient arrived with missing labs, and one operating room turnover took longer because a sterilizer alarm stopped the team.

The result tells you what happened; the postmortem asks whether the process deserved that result.

Rosa separates the decision from the noise around it. The new schedule correctly placed the highest-risk case first. The lab checklist missed a known weak point. The sterilizer alarm was outside the scheduling decision. That split matters because each piece teaches a different lesson. Keep the case-ordering rule. Change the prearrival lab check. Do not redesign the whole schedule because one machine failed.

The work is feedback, postmortem, reflection, and improvement with discipline. Reflection is not replaying the pain until someone feels guilty. A postmortem should ask: what did we know, what did we assume, what mattered, what was noise, and which rule should improve? Without that split, experience becomes superstition.

The lesson should be smaller than the story.

The limit is defensiveness. Process review can become a way to excuse every bad result as bad luck. If the same pattern repeats, stop calling it noise. Repetition is feedback.
breakdown.fullRead:
"The pilot missed the target," Ines says while the grant report sits open beside returned participant forms. Before the review, the team wants to label the program a failure. After she separates process from result, the picture changes. Recruitment was strong, attendance was weak during the transit strike, and the strongest gains came from participants who received reminder calls.

The result alone says under target. The learning says three different things. The outreach process worked. The attendance plan was fragile. Reminder calls may be worth building into the next version. If Ines treats the whole pilot as failure, she throws away useful signal with the disappointing number.

Good learning has to resist two temptations. The first is outcome worship: if it worked, repeat everything. The second is outcome panic: if it failed, change everything. Both are lazy because they let the result do all the thinking.

Look at your own last outcome. What part came from the quality of the decision? What part came from execution? What part came from luck, timing, weather, market movement, illness, a supplier, or one person having a bad day? If you cannot separate those, you will either overlearn or underlearn.

The audition hall is empty when Vera stacks the youth orchestra score sheets beside the final seating chart. In reflection, she sees that the strongest violinist did not win the first-chair spot. That result could make the panel rewrite the audition process. Instead, Vera reviews the notes. The panel weighted sight-reading heavily because the season required new music every week. The stronger performer had a beautiful prepared piece and weak sight-reading. The process matched the season's needs. The upset result was not proof of error.

You are looking at Joana's product launch retrospective with launch-day screenshots on one side and support tickets on the other. She must decide before the next release planning meeting: treat the launch as a success because signups were high, or inspect the process that produced those signups. The thought experiment exposes the trap. Paid ads drove a spike, but onboarding failed for the customers most likely to stay. The result looked good; the process leaked the future.

It took Isabel one winter to understand the property purchase postmortem. The house rose in value, so everyone congratulated the decision. Then a probate delay, a roof leak, and a surprise easement showed how thin the process had been. Before bidding on the next property, Isabel must decide whether to repeat the win or keep only the parts that deserved trust: neighborhood research, financing discipline, and inspection rules that need to be stricter.

Experience improves judgment only when you read it carefully. Do not let a good outcome bless a poor process. Do not let a bad outcome bury a sound one. Write the update in one precise sentence: keep this rule, change this check, ignore this noise, or gather better evidence next time.

examples.title: The Profitable Accident

planSpec.audience: investors separating lucky results from repeatable process
planSpec.stakes: Teresa can turn a profitable accident into a dangerous rule.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Teresa separates the good return from the weak purchase process before updating the club rule.

examples.scenario: The receipt paper curls beside Teresa's coffee cup while the investment club celebrates a stock that doubled. The room is already turning the win into wisdom, and someone has written "founder conviction" at the top of next month's screening list. Before they write a new buying rule, she must choose between learning from the profit and reviewing the process. The reveal is uncomfortable: the result was good, but the notes show no margin check, no comparison, and no balance-sheet review.
examples.whatToDo: Separate result from process before updating the rule. Teresa should record the win as lucky until the process earns trust.
examples.whyItMatters: A good outcome can reward a weak method. Repeating the method may turn one lucky result into future damage.

examples.title: The Three Delays

planSpec.audience: hospital teams learning from delays without overcorrecting
planSpec.stakes: Rosa can blame the schedule or separate rule failure, checklist gap, and random equipment alarm.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rosa keeps the case-ordering rule, changes the lab check, and ignores the sterilizer alarm as schedule noise.

examples.scenario: At 7:30 Monday, Rosa opens the surgery audit and sees three delayed cases from Friday. The first comment in the review thread says the new schedule failed, but the notes show three different mechanisms hiding under one bad morning. In the postmortem, she splits the causes: the new case-ordering rule worked, the prearrival lab checklist missed a weak point, and a sterilizer alarm was noise outside scheduling. Only one rule needs changing.
examples.whatToDo: Sort each result into process, execution gap, or noise. Rosa should change the lab check without redesigning the whole schedule.
examples.whyItMatters: Bad outcomes often contain several causes. Learning improves when each cause gets the right update.

examples.title: The Under-Target Pilot

planSpec.audience: program leads interpreting disappointing results without discarding useful signal
planSpec.stakes: Ines can label the pilot a failure or preserve the parts that worked.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Ines separates outreach strength, transit-strike attendance noise, and reminder-call signal.

examples.scenario: "The pilot missed the target," Ines says while returned participant forms sit beside the grant report. The funder wants a simple answer, and the team is tempted to file the whole effort under failure before anyone reads the attendance notes. Before reflection, the team calls it failure. After she separates process from result, outreach looks strong, a transit strike explains attendance noise, and reminder calls appear to improve completion.
examples.whatToDo: Turn the outcome into specific updates. Ines should keep outreach, strengthen attendance resilience, and test reminder calls.
examples.whyItMatters: A disappointing result can still contain useful process signal. Treating everything as failure wastes what the pilot taught.

examples.title: The Sight-Reading Weight

planSpec.audience: judges reviewing surprising results without abandoning sound criteria
planSpec.stakes: Vera can overreact to an upset result or confirm that the criteria matched the season's needs.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Vera sees that sight-reading weighting matched the season even though the prepared-piece favorite lost.

examples.scenario: The audition hall is empty when Vera stacks score sheets beside the final seating chart. Parents are surprised by the winner, and one colleague says the panel may have overthought the criteria. In reflection, the upset result bothers her until she reviews the criteria. The first-chair winner had weaker prepared tone but stronger sight-reading, and the season requires new music every week. The process matched the need.
examples.whatToDo: Check whether the criteria fit the original goal before changing them. Vera should not rewrite the process only because the result surprised people.
examples.whyItMatters: A surprising outcome is not automatically a bad decision. Sometimes it proves the criteria were doing their job.

examples.title: The Signup Spike

planSpec.audience: teams learning from strong launch numbers without ignoring weak process
planSpec.stakes: Joana can mistake high signups for proof while onboarding leaks future retention.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Joana distinguishes paid-ad signup noise from onboarding process weakness.

examples.scenario: You look at Joana's launch screenshots while support tickets pile up beside the retention chart. The marketing dashboard is green, the investor update is drafted, and the product team wants to call the launch system proven. She must decide before the next release meeting: call the launch a win because signups spiked or inspect the process. Imagine paid ads vanish tomorrow. The signup result shrinks, and the onboarding leak becomes the real lesson.
examples.whatToDo: Ask which part of the result will repeat without the lucky push. Joana should update onboarding, not celebrate the whole launch system.
examples.whyItMatters: Strong numbers can hide weak process. Learning requires asking what created the result and whether it can repeat.

examples.title: The Rising House

planSpec.audience: buyers separating profitable outcomes from risky process
planSpec.stakes: Isabel can repeat a profitable purchase process that hid serious risks.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Isabel keeps neighborhood research but tightens probate, roof, and easement checks before the next bid.

examples.scenario: It took Isabel one winter to see that the rising house price had covered a thin process. The appraisal looked brilliant after the market moved, but the old file still showed a missed probate delay, a roof note she had skimmed, and an easement question nobody had answered. Before the next bid, she must decide whether to repeat the win or review the purchase. The speakerphone sits beside the probate folder as she keeps the neighborhood research and tightens probate, roof, and easement checks.
examples.whatToDo: Do not let profit bless every step. Isabel should keep the process parts that earned trust and strengthen the checks that were lucky.
examples.whyItMatters: A profitable purchase can still reveal weak judgment. The postmortem keeps gain from becoming overconfidence.

questions.prompt: An investment club made money on a stock bought after a confident founder interview, with no margin check or balance-sheet review. What should the club learn?
choices: Confident founder interviews are a reliable buying signal.
The result was good, but the process was weak and should not become the rule.
Profitable picks do not need postmortems.
questions.explanation: The gain does not prove the process. The club should separate lucky outcome from a rule that lacks evidence and margin checks.

questions.prompt: A surgery schedule produced three delays. One was an emergency add-on, one came from missing labs, and one came from a sterilizer alarm. What update is strongest?
choices: Abandon the new schedule because delays happened.
Keep the case-ordering rule, improve the lab checklist, and do not blame scheduling for the sterilizer alarm.
Tell staff that Friday was unlucky and change nothing.
questions.explanation: This separates process, checklist gap, and noise. Abandoning everything overreacts, while changing nothing ignores the lab signal.

questions.prompt: A grant pilot missed its target during a transit strike, but outreach was strong and reminder calls improved completion. What should the review conclude?
choices: The pilot failed and should be discarded.
The pilot succeeded because at least one part worked.
Keep outreach, strengthen attendance resilience, and test reminder calls again.
questions.explanation: The conclusion turns mixed feedback into precise updates. Full rejection and full praise both flatten the evidence.

questions.prompt: A youth orchestra's first-chair winner surprised parents. The panel weighted sight-reading heavily because the season requires new music weekly. How should the panel interpret this?
choices: The upset result proves the audition process was unfair.
The process may be sound if the criteria matched the season's actual demands.
Prepared pieces should always outweigh sight-reading.
questions.explanation: The result is surprising, not automatically wrong. The key is whether the process criteria fit the decision goal.

questions.prompt: A product launch had high signups because paid ads spiked traffic, but onboarding tickets show many new users got stuck. What is the best learning?
choices: The launch process worked because signups were high.
Paid ads should be treated as noise around acquisition, while onboarding needs process improvement.
The launch failed completely because support tickets rose.
questions.explanation: This separates the visible result from the process that affects durable customers. Both celebration and panic would misread the feedback.

questions.prompt: A property purchase rose in value, but the buyer missed a probate delay, roof issue, and easement risk. What should she update before buying again?
choices: Repeat the process because the investment made money.
Avoid property because one profitable purchase had hidden problems.
Keep the strong neighborhood research and tighten probate, roof, and easement checks.
questions.explanation: The profit should not bless weak checks. The update preserves what worked and repairs what luck covered.

questions.prompt: A team reviews a failed project and writes, "Bad luck," even though the same handoff problem has appeared in four projects. What is the issue?
choices: Repeated patterns are feedback, not noise.
Any failed outcome proves the whole process is broken.
Postmortems should avoid uncomfortable details.
questions.explanation: One event can be noise, but repetition is signal. Calling the same problem luck prevents improvement.

questions.prompt: A manager wants to reward every tactic used in a successful campaign. Which question would improve the learning?
choices: Which parts of the process would we trust if the result had been average?
Which person deserves credit for the good result?
How can we make the next campaign feel equally exciting?
questions.explanation: This question tests process quality apart from the result. Credit and excitement do not reveal which rules should repeat.

questions.prompt: A sales team loses a deal after following a strong qualification process, but the buyer's budget was frozen by a surprise merger. What should the review avoid?
choices: Changing the qualification process solely because this result was bad.
Asking whether any early merger signs were missed.
Recording the budget freeze as a factor in the decision log.
questions.explanation: A bad result caused by external noise should not automatically rewrite a sound process. Checking for missed signs is still useful.

reviewCards.front: A result is loud, but the cause is unclear. What is the first split in learning from a decision?
reviewCards.back: Separate process, result, and noise before turning the experience into a rule.

reviewCards.front: Why can a good result be dangerous?
reviewCards.back: It can make a weak process look trustworthy, causing you to repeat luck as if it were skill.

reviewCards.front: Why can a bad result be misleading?
reviewCards.back: A sound process can still meet bad luck, external shocks, or normal variance. Do not punish it automatically.

reviewCards.front: When should you stop calling something noise?
reviewCards.back: When the pattern repeats. Repetition turns excuse into feedback that deserves a process update.
A precise update: keep this rule, change this check, ignore this noise, or gather better evidence next time.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is reading outcomes without worshiping or panicking over them. You practice splitting process, result, and noise before updating rules.

ifThenPlans.plan: If an outcome went well, then I will ask which process steps deserved trust before repeating them.
If an outcome went poorly, then I will identify what was process failure, execution gap, and noise before changing the rule.
If a review becomes blame or celebration, then I will return it to what we knew, assumed, missed, and should update.
If the same problem appears twice, then I will stop labeling it luck and inspect the process.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Review one recent decision and write one sentence each for process quality, result, noise, and the rule update.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Keep a decision log and revisit one entry each week to ask whether the outcome changed your rule for the right reason.

memorableLines.text: A lucky win can become an expensive teacher.
memorableLines.why: It warns against learning the wrong lesson from success.

memorableLines.text: The result tells you what happened; the postmortem asks whether the process deserved that result.
memorableLines.why: It states the chapter's central separation.

memorableLines.text: The lesson should be smaller than the story.
memorableLines.why: It keeps learning precise rather than sweeping.
